questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273897/assets/2a89a14bced6f6700614cfad216070154cae165785458f817ea06d266edfde4e.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,dy & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273897/assets/0a60729b626e1e9e219a839898cacc18aa81ec2a9b1b445e7b92b721874c2550.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273897/assets/c5eb703c2812d82848bb5a1639c2840c4abf9318b988087e2216d9881137da72.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{4}\,i+{t}^{3}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=\,i-t\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{8}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
